title: Hydras of the World
text:
Arguably the most comprehensive molecular phylogeny of the genus Hydra to date was published by Martínez et al. (2010). Their study evaluated 102 strains—primarily collected from wild populations, alongside widely used laboratory strains such as 105, Zurich, and AEP. Notably, the analysis also incorporated strains sampled directly from the type localities of H. carnea and H. littoralis. While readers are strongly encouraged to consult the full paper, key findings are summarized below:

Green and brown hydras represent two distinct monophyletic groups and are sister lineages.
Within the brown hydras, Oligactis and Vulgaris are sister lineages, while Braueri is the most early-diverging.
Eight distinct clades were found which correspond to 8 morphologically described species. They are: Hydra viridissima, Hydra utahensis, Hydra circumcincta, Hydra hymanae, Hydra oligactis, Hydra canadensis, Hydra oxycnida and Hydra vulgaris.
Campbell’s (1987) clustering of hydras into four groups is supported by this phylogeny; that is, the groups represent true clades (groups of hydra sharing a common ancestor).
The Viridissima Group includes all green hydra, H. viridissima The Braueri group includes H. hymanae, H. utahensis, and H. circumcincta. The Oligactis group includes H. oligactis, H. canadensis, and H. oxycnida. And the Vulgaris group includes H. vulgaris. Also included in this group are H. carnea, H.littoralis, and H. magnipapillata strain 105. These species are nested well inside the group and cannot be distinguished from other strains; nothing in the tree suggests that they should be considered a different species.
Since its description by Schulze (1914), H. circumcincta has been considered a European hydra. However, its discovery in Alaska suggests that H. circumcincta may have a circumpolar distribution.
Only two of the nine species of hydras, H. viridissima and H. vulgaris, occur on continents derived from Gondwana—landmasses that today contain large territories south of the Equator1.
Based on that observation (7.), the authors suggest an important hypotheses: Hydras originated in Laurasia and the only two species capable of colonizing the Gondwana-derived continents were H. viridissima and H. vulgaris because of their higher tolerance to temperature (Bosch et al. 1988, Gellner et al. 1992, Ye el at. 2019).






Maximum Likelihood Phylogram from Martinez et a. 2010. Please click on the image to enlarge it and inspect specific details



Bosch, T. C. G., Krylow, S. M., Bode, H. R., & Steele, R. E. (1988). Thermotolerance and synthesis of heat shock proteins in the freshwater cnidarian Hydra. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 85(21), 7927–7931. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.85.21.7927


A classic comparative study establishing that Hydra oligactis lacks an inducible heat-shock response (HSR) and is extremely sensitive to elevated temperatures (disintegrating above 24–33°C), whereas Hydra attenuata (H. vulgaris) synthesizes major heat-shock proteins (Hsps, notably Hsp60 and Hsp70) and acquires thermotolerance following pre-incubation at sub-lethal elevated temperatures. [AI Gemini]

Gellner, K., Praetzel, G., & Bosch, T. C. G. (1992). Cloning and expression of a heat-inducible hsp70 gene in two species of Hydra which differ in their stress response. European Journal of Biochemistry, 210(3), 683–691. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1432-1033.1992.tb17469.x


Investigates the molecular mechanics underlying the divergence in thermal tolerance between H. vulgaris and H. oligactis, demonstrating transcriptional differences in hsp70 expression under thermal stress.[AI Gemini]

Martínez, D. E., Iñiguez, A. R., Percell, K. M., Willner, J. B., Signorovitch, J., & Campbell, R. D. (2010). Phylogeny and biogeography of Hydra (Cnidaria: Hydridae) using mitochondrial and nuclear DNA sequences. Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution, 57(1), 403–410. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ympev.2010.06.012
Schulze, P. (1914). Bestimmungstabelle der deutschen Hydraarten (Vorläufige Mitteilung). Sitzungsberichte der Gesellschaft Naturforschender Freunde zu Berlin, 1914(9), 395–398.
Ye, S., Badhiwala, K. N., Robinson, J. T., Cho, W. H., & Siemann, E. (2019). Thermal plasticity of a freshwater cnidarian holobiont: detection of trans-generational effects in asexually reproducing hosts and symbionts. The ISME Journal, 13(8), 2058–2067. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41396-019-0413-0


Explores the upper thermal limits and acclimation dynamics in Hydra viridissima (green hydra). The paper measures critical thermal maxima (CTM) and disintegration times at 37–38°C, assessing how host-symbiont interactions (symbiotic vs. aposymbiotic states) and thermal history alter whole-organism heat tolerance.

title: Hydras of the World
text:
Hydra species and clades

Hydras are freshwater invertebrates belonging to the phylum Cnidaria, a group of animals that also includes corals, sea anemones, and jellyfish. While the vast majority of cnidarians are marine, hydras are among the few species adapted to freshwater environments. Within the class Aplanulata—which is characterized by the absence of the typical planula larva stage found in other hydroids—all species of the Genus Hydra are classified into their own dedicated family, Hydridae. Widely distributed across the globe, hydras inhabit ponds, lakes, and rivers. Although they thrive best in cold water, different species exhibit varying degrees of tolerance to warmer environments. As carnivorous predators, they feed on small crustaceans, insect larvae, and even fish fry. Hydra reproduce both sexually and asexually (by budding). Some species are gonochoristic (dioecious) with male or female individuals, while most hydras are hermaphroditic producing both testes and eggs.
Tens of different species of hydras have been proposed based on morphological characters and geographical origin. However, molecular phylogenies suggest that the number of species is rather small. We have identified nine distinct species: Hydra viridissima, Hydra utahensis, Hydra circumcincta, Hydra hymanae, Hydra oligactis, Hydra canadensis, Hydra oxycnida, Hydra lirosoma, and Hydra vulgaris.
The nine hydra species maybe grouped into five distinct clades (see Campbell’s groups): Viridissima, Braueri, Oligactis, Lirosoma, and Vulgaris. The Viridissima clade includes the “green” hydras, which harbor intracellular green unicellular algae within their endodermal epithelial cells, while the remaining four clades comprise the “brown” hydras. Interestingly, the genomes of the brown hydras are approximately three times the size of the genomes of the green hydras as the result of the expansion of long interspersed nuclear elements, mostly of a single family of the chicken repeat 1 (CR1) class (Wong et al. 2019).
While most animal taxa feature a single, circular mitochondrial chromosome, linear mitochondrial genomes have evolved independently in a few lineages, including hydras, box jellyfish, and calcareous sponges. In the Vulgaris clade of hydras the mitochondrial genome is split into two linear chromosomes (each roughly 8 kb in size). In all the other four clades, there is a single linear chromosome of ~16 kb.



The distribution of hydra species throughout the world is quite interesting. While all nine species can be found on continents derived from Laurasia, only two species—H. viridissima and H. vulgaris—natively inhabit the southern hemisphere continents derived from Gondwana1. This observation led Martínez et al. (2010) to suggest that hydras evolved in Laurasia, a hypothesis supported by the current estimated times of divergence among Hydra clades (Wong et al. 2019). Furthermore, these two Southern Hemisphere species appear to exhibit a higher tolerance to elevated temperatures, which may explain their broader global distribution.

Martínez D.E. , A.R. Iñiguez; K.M. Percell; J.B. Willner; J. Signorovitch; R.D. Campbell, 2010. Phylogeny and biogeography of Hydra (Cnidaria: Hydridae) using mitochondrial and nuclear DNA sequences. Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 57 (20): 403-410.
Wong W.Y., O. Simakov, D.M. Bridge , P. Cartwright , A.J. Bellantuono , A. Kuhn , T. Holstein , C. David , R.E. Steele , D.E. Martínez, 2019. Expansion of a single transposable element family is associated with genome size increase and radiation in the genus Hydra. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA. 116 (46): 22915–22917.

title: About these visualizations
text:
This website and the visualizations here were created as assignments for the Foundations of Data Science in R course taught by Professor Jo Hardin at Pomona College.
I audited the class in the fall of 2026 and I absolutely loved the course. I am indebted to Professor Hardin, who gracefully allowed my unusual presence in her classroom. I am also grateful to my students Ava Santos-Volpe and Ryan (bRyan) Mooney who insisted that I take this class; they knew I would love it.
The visualizations presented here represent assignments designed for students to learn various data science concepts. Students were free to select TidyTuesday datasets to analyze and display. I chose datasets on Orca Encounters in Puget Sound, Dear Abby letters, and Palmtrees to practice different types of graphs.

title: About these visualizations
text:
TidyTuesday
What is TidyTuesday? A response from AI (Gemini)
TidyTuesday is a weekly data project aimed at the R community, hosted by the R4DS Online Learning Community (Data Science in a Box / R for Data Science).
Every Tuesday, a new dataset is posted on GitHub, usually accompanied by a brief article or chart exploring it. Participants from around the world download the data, analyze it, create data visualizations (most commonly using ggplot2), and share their code and plots on social media (primarily on X/Twitter and LinkedIn) using the hashtag #TidyTuesday.

Key Features of TidyTuesday

Focus on the “Tidyverse”: The project encourages the use of tidy data principles and packages from the tidyverse ecosystem (like dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2), though participants are free to use any tools or programming languages they prefer.
Real-World Data: The datasets cover a wide variety of engaging, often quirky topics—ranging from historical events and scientific discoveries to pop culture, sports, and environmental statistics.
Learning and Community: It serves as a low-stakes, supportive environment for beginners and experienced data scientists alike to practice data wrangling, sharpen data visualization skills, and learn from how others approach the same dataset.

text:
Hola! I am Daniel Martínez Scavino, a biology professor at Pomona College. My research centers on Hydra—the remarkable, biologically immortal organism that somehow missed the memo on aging. When I am not in the lab or teaching Introductory Genetics or Genomics & Transcriptomics, you can usually find me exploring mountain trails, traveling, cooking, or diving into new languages. I was born in Argentina so my native language is Spanish.

title: Hydras of the World
text:
Species distribution
The map below displays the locations of hydra collected throughout the world. These hydras were identified by sequencing the Internal Transcribed Spacers (ITS-1 and ITS-2) of ribosomal DNA. This marker is very effective to distinguish between different species because the sequences are quite distinct (Martínez et al, 2010). When possible the identification was corroborated by looking at morphological traits like nematocysts (mainly stenoteles and holotrychous isorhizas), embryothecae, and tentacle emergence in buds (see the key to identify clades for additional details).
Please use your computer pad to enlarge the zone you want to observe. There is little we can do about the map projection which distorts the true areas of the world exaggerating lands at higher latitudes.

title: Dear Abby
text:
Husbands vs Wifes
The word “husband” is consistenly one of the most frequently used in these letters throughout several decades. Is that because women are the main writters to Abby? In order to investigate this a bit further, I have selected letters that include the words “my husband” and “my wife” hoping that this indentifies the writer. This is obviously not a perfect strategy. The word clouds below come from those letters. Assuming that the writers are talking about their partners, what can the word frequencies tell us about the letters? Are the themes different? Have they changed through time?

title: Hydras of the World
text:
Hydra species lists
Many new species of hydra have been proposed since the first hydra, Hydra oligactis, was described by Antonie Philips van Leeuwenhoek in a letter sent to the Royal Society of London in 1702 (The letter was published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London a year later–Van Leeuwenhoek, 1703). The few distinct morphological traits of hydra make it difficult to distinguish between species and consequently to describe new ones. While reading descriptions of many new species, one is tempted to assume that these new species were proposed simply based on their geographical origin. The figure below shows three lists of species from papers by Ewer (1948), Grayson (1971), and Campbell (1987). The number of “valid” species included in these lists varies significantly. One of the best analysis of the validity of hydra species is the paper by Campbell (1987). Anyone with interest on hydra taxonomy is encourage to read that paper. A phylogenetic study using molecular markers and including more than 102 strains collected from around the world (Martínez et al. 2010), suggests that the number of species maybe much smaller. There seem to be 9 distinct “molecular” clades (monophyletic groups) of hydra which correspond to 9 previously described morphological species.
  
Peter Simon Pallas (1741–1811) was a prominent German zoologist and botanist who spent a large portion of his career working in the Russian Empire. He is widely recognized as one of the great naturalists and explorers of the 18th and early 19th centuries.

Palm trees can be tall! Or very short…
Palm trees are quite variable in height ranging from 0 to 170 meters. Palm tress can be grouped by Tribes (a taxonomic rank between family and genus). Members of some tribes are taller than trees in other tribes. Calameae and Lepidocaryeae are two tribes with particularly tall trees.

title: Hydras of the World
text:
Campbell’s groups
Building on Schulze’s (1917) idea that hydra can be clustered into morphological types, Campbell (1987) established four groups of hydra: the Viridissima group (green hydras), the Braueri group (gracile hydras), the Oligactis group (stalked hydras) and the Vulgaris group (common hydras). Campbell summarized the distinct morphological traits of these groups into an identification key. In the same paper, Campbell described a new species, H. lirosoma, collected from a creek near the Okefenokee Swamp in southern Georgia, USA.
Although Campbell placed H. lirosoma in the Braueri group due to the broad shape of its holotrichous isorhiza nematocysts, he noted that it differs from other group members “by virtue of its spherical embryotheca, other species usually have flattened embryothecae that adhere to the substratum.” Subsequent genomic characterization indicates that H. lirosoma actually represents an entirely distinct group of hydra. The identification key below has been modified from Campbell (1987) to reflect this updated taxonomic status.
It is important to note that Campbell’s groups were confirmed to correspond to monophyletic groups (clades) of hydra (Martínez et al. 2010).

title: Orca Encounters
text:
Orcas are nasty fish that enjoy munching on people!
Nope! There are several things that are wrong with that picture. Orcas are cetaceans related to dolphins that live in all of the world oceans. They are higly intelligent predators that hunt in coordinated family pods using very elaborate strategies. Their varied diet includes fish, sharks, smaller marine mammals (e.g. see lions), and even whales. But not humans!

title: Hydras of the World
text:
The main objective of this project is to provide a comprehensive resource for anyone interested in the global diversity of Hydra. Understanding this diversity within an evolutionary framework is essential for researchers working with the genus. While modern biology has made remarkable progress by focusing on standard model organisms, an overwhelming skew toward a tiny handful of species creates a severely distorted view of life—a distinct taxonomic bias.
Hydra researchers often describe their study subjects as “non-model organisms,” yet they frequently generalize findings based on a single laboratory strain of sometimes uncertain origin. Variation is the norm, not the exception. While every study obviously cannot include multiple strains or species, these pages aim to encourage colleagues to rigorously characterize the taxonomic status of the strains they study rather than simply reporting a species name without any additional information.
Compounding this issue, evidence shows that standard laboratory strains—such as Hydra vulgaris 105 and Hydra vulgaris AEP—have significantly diverged since being collected and maintained across different laboratories worldwide for over 40 and 30 years, respectively. Very likely, these laboratory cultures regularly experience genetic bottlenecks and artificial selection in captivity. Keep in mind this potential source of variation when reporting work on a given species and strain.
Understanding the diversity and distribution of Hydra around the world requires a monumental effort, and no one contributed more to this enterprise than Dr. Richard D. Campbell at University of California, Irvine. Campbell collected specimens from approximately 2,000 distinct locations across every unfrozen continent, resolving numerous taxonomic complexities and clarifying the validity of many species (e.g. Campbell 1987, 1989; Campbell & Holstein, 1991; Holstein, Campbell & Tardent, 1990).
Dr. Robert Steele (UCI) and I have completed several collecting trips in search of hydras. I am deeply grateful for Rob’s companionship and support, especially in some extraordinary destinations like the Peruvian highlands, the Peruvian Amazon, northern Mexico, the Okefenokee Swamp in Georgia, and the Great Dismal Swamp in Virginia.
More recently, Callen Hyland at the University of San Diego has spearheaded an iNaturalist project to map global observations.
